displayQuote: Talent does what it can; genius does what it must

meta.title: Who really said "Talent does what it can; genius does what it must"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not the novelist Edward Bulwer-Lytton — the line is his son Robert’s (‘Owen Meredith’), and the popular version reverses the original couplet.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Talent does what it can; genius does what it must'?
meta.ogDescription: The line belongs to Robert Bulwer-Lytton (‘Owen Meredith’), not his father — whose poem reads “Genius does what it must, and Talent does what it can.”

answer.label: Not Edward Bulwer-Lytton — his son, ‘Owen Meredith’
answer.authorDates: 1831–1891 · Poet ‘Owen Meredith’; son of novelist Edward Bulwer-Lytton
answer.sourceLine: The line really is a Bulwer-Lytton’s — but the son’s, not the father’s. It comes from Robert Bulwer-Lytton’s poem “Last Words,” first printed in the Cornhill Magazine (Nov 1860) and collected in Chronicles and Characters (1868), where it reads “Genius does what it must, and Talent does what it can.” The everyday form reverses the two clauses and pins the line on his far more famous father, the novelist Edward Bulwer-Lytton.

source.heading: The primary source
source.excerpt:
Talk not of genius baffled. Genius is master of man;
Genius does what it must, and Talent does what it can.
Blot out my name, that the spirits of Shakespeare and Milton and Burns
Look not down on the praises of fools with a pity my soul yet spurns.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section traces the line to Chronicles and Characters (1868), Vol. ii, p. 302 — the work of the son, Robert.
Wikiquote’s Genius page prints the full stanza and dates its first appearance to the Cornhill Magazine, Nov 1860.
The University of Iowa’s LUCILE Project confirms ‘Owen Meredith’ was Edward Robert Bulwer-Lytton (1831–1891), son of the novelist.
Quote sites such as Goodreads still file the reversed wording under the father, Edward.
source.excerptNote: The couplet in its original order — genius first, talent second. The circulated version flips the two clauses.
source.rightsNote: First printed in 1860 and collected in 1868, with its author dead since 1891, the poem has been in the public domain in the United States for well over a century.

author.name: Robert Bulwer-Lytton
author.heading: About the real author
author.bio: Robert Bulwer-Lytton published his verse under the pen name Owen Meredith while pursuing a diplomatic career that made him Viceroy of India (1876–1880) and later ambassador to France. He was the son of the far more famous novelist Edward Bulwer-Lytton — a proximity that has repeatedly caused this couplet to be reassigned to his father. Critics judged him prolific but uneven; this line from “Last Words” is among his most enduring.

misattribution.heading: A famous line, credited to the wrong Lytton
misattribution.intro: This one is misattributed twice over: to the wrong man, and in the wrong words.

items.why: The novelist who gave us “It was a dark and stormy night” is the name almost every quotation site attaches to this line — Goodreads and BrainyQuote among them. But he was the father; the line is his son’s.

items.who: “Talent does what it can; genius does what it must”
items.why: The circulated form flips the couplet’s order. As Wikiquote records the original, it reads “Genius does what it must, and Talent does what it can.”

misattribution.truthLine: The true author is Robert Bulwer-Lytton, ‘Owen Meredith,’ in his poem “Last Words” (Chronicles and Characters, 1868).

context.heading: Why the line endures
lead: The couplet has become shorthand for a Romantic idea: that true genius is compelled rather than merely capable, and its force comes from the contrast between the two clauses. There is a small irony in its afterlife — a line about genius ‘doing what it must’ has spent a century and a half being made to do what quotation culture wants, reworded and reassigned to a more marketable name.
context.pull: “Genius does what it must, and Talent does what it can.”
